rows.question: How are redirects followed, and where is the maximum number of redirects enforced?
rows.answer: Redirects are followed by SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects, a generator that loops while a redirect target exists: it copies the request, appends the previous response to history, consumes/releases the connection, normalizes the URL (handling scheme-less "//" URLs and preserving fragments), then calls self.send with allow_redirects=False and extracts the next redirect target via get_redirect_target (src/requests/sessions.py:186-235, src/requests/sessions.py:282-307). The redirect target is obtained from the response's Location header when resp.is_redirect (src/requests/sessions.py:127-152). The maximum number of redirects is enforced inside resolve_redirects: if len(resp.history) >= self.max_redirects it raises TooManyRedirects (src/requests/sessions.py:186-235); the TooManyRedirects exception is defined in src/requests/exceptions.py:102-162. Session.send invokes resolve_redirects when allow_redirects is true (src/requests/sessions.py:801-829).

rows.question: Where is the Authorization header removed when a redirect goes to a different host?
rows.answer: The Authorization header is removed in SessionRedirectMixin.rebuild_auth, which deletes headers["Authorization"] when should_strip_auth returns True for a redirect to a different host (src/requests/sessions.py:309-332). The decision to strip is made in should_strip_auth, which returns True when the old and new hostnames differ (src/requests/sessions.py:154-184).

arguments.query: Authorization header removed redirect different host

rows.question: How does a POST request become a GET after a 303 See Other redirect?
rows.answer: When a redirect response is received, SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects copies the original prepared request and calls self.rebuild_method(prepared_request, resp) to adjust the method (src/requests/sessions.py:237-280). rebuild_method checks the response status code and, per RFC 7231 section 6.4.4, if the status is 303 See Other and the original method is not HEAD, it sets the method to GET (src/requests/sessions.py:370-392). After the method is changed, resolve_redirects also purges the Content-Length, Content-Type, and Transfer-Encoding headers and sets the body to None for redirects other than 307/308, so the new GET request is sent without the original POST body (src/requests/sessions.py:237-280).

arguments.query: 303 See Other redirect POST GET method change

rows.question: How are automatic retries configured for the connection pool?
rows.answer: Automatic retries for the connection pool are configured through the HTTPAdapter's max_retries parameter. In __init__, if max_retries equals DEFAULT_RETRIES, self.max_retries is set to Retry(0, read=False) (no retries); otherwise it is set via Retry.from_int(max_retries) (src/requests/adapters.py:201-237). The class docstring explains that max_retries is the maximum number of retries each connection should attempt, applies only to failed DNS lookups, socket connections and connection timeouts (never to requests where data reached the server), and that by default Requests does not retry failed connections; for granular control you can pass a urllib3 Retry object instead (src/requests/adapters.py:158-199). The pool itself is created in init_poolmanager, which builds a urllib3 PoolManager with num_pools, maxsize and block, but retries are not passed there—they are handled by the adapter's max_retries (src/requests/adapters.py:239-267).

arguments.query: automatic retries connection pool retry configuration

rows.question: Where are SSL certificates verified and the CA bundle chosen?
rows.answer: SSL certificate verification is performed in HTTPAdapter.cert_verify, which sets conn.cert_reqs to CERT_REQUIRED for https URLs when verify is truthy, and chooses the CA bundle from the user-supplied verify path if given, otherwise from DEFAULT_CA_BUNDLE_PATH, setting conn.ca_certs for a file or conn.ca_cert_dir for a directory (src/requests/adapters.py:307-363). The default CA bundle is provided by the certifi package via where() in src/requests/certs.py:1-18.

rows.question: How is the response body decoded into text when the server sends no charset?
rows.answer: When the server sends no charset, Response.text falls back to self.apparent_encoding, which guesses the encoding using charset_normalizer or chardet, and then decodes the bytes with that encoding (or utf-8 if still None) using errors='replace' (src/requests/models.py:1055-1089). The header-based encoding is obtained via get_encoding_from_headers, which returns None when there is no content-type or no charset parameter, and only defaults to ISO-8859-1 for text/* or utf-8 for application/json (src/requests/utils.py:569-587).

arguments.query: decode response body charset text encoding

rows.question: How does streaming a download in chunks work?
rows.answer: Streaming a download in chunks is done by Response.iter_content, which yields the response body in pieces instead of loading it all into memory (src/requests/models.py:914-965). When the request was made with stream=True, the inner generate() function reads from the underlying urllib3 raw stream via self.raw.stream(chunk_size, decode_content=True), yielding each chunk as it arrives; if the raw object is a standard file-like object it instead loops calling self.raw.read(chunk_size) until an empty chunk is returned (src/requests/models.py:914-965). The chunk_size argument is the number of bytes to read into memory per chunk, and it must be an int or None; None means read data as it arrives when stream=True, or return the whole body as a single chunk when stream=False (src/requests/models.py:914-965). If the content was already consumed, iter_content simulates small chunks by slicing the stored bytes with iter_slices (src/requests/models.py:967-977). When decode_unicode is True, the byte chunks are passed through stream_decode_response_unicode, which uses an incremental decoder based on the response encoding to yield decoded text, falling back to raw bytes if no encoding is available (src/requests/utils.py:596-611). The stream flag is set on the request via Session.request, which passes it into the adapter's send (src/requests/sessions.py:601-653).

rows.question: How is JSON parsed from a response, and what error is raised if the body is not valid JSON?
rows.answer: Response.json decodes the body with complexjson.loads (an alias for the json/simplejson module). If no encoding is set and the content is longer than 3 bytes, it first guesses the UTF variant via guess_json_utf and tries to decode the raw bytes; a UnicodeDecodeError is swallowed and it falls through to decoding self.text. In either path, a JSONDecodeError is caught and re-raised as requests.exceptions.JSONDecodeError (RequestsJSONDecodeError), constructed with the original error's msg, doc and pos (src/requests/models.py:1091-1142). That exception subclasses InvalidJSONError and the compat JSONDecodeError, so it is both a RequestException and a JSON decode error (src/requests/exceptions.py:42-66).

arguments.query: parse JSON from response body invalid JSON error

rows.question: Where is HTTP Digest authentication implemented?
rows.answer: HTTP Digest authentication is implemented in the HTTPDigestAuth class in src/requests/auth.py:124-155, which defines the class and its per-thread state initialization. The digest header is built in build_digest_header (src/requests/auth.py:157-266), the request is prepared and hooks are registered in __call__ (src/requests/auth.py:321-354), and the 401 challenge is handled in handle_401 (src/requests/auth.py:268-319).

rows.question: How is the value of the Basic auth header built?
rows.answer: The Basic auth header value is built by _basic_auth_str, which first coerces non-string username/password to str (with a deprecation warning), then encodes any str username and password to bytes using latin1, joins them with a colon, base64-encodes the result, strips whitespace, converts it to a native string, and prefixes it with 'Basic ' (src/requests/auth.py:34-82). HTTPBasicAuth.__call__ assigns this value to the Authorization header, and HTTPProxyAuth.__call__ assigns it to Proxy-Authorization (src/requests/auth.py:85-121).

rows.question: How does the library decide whether a URL should bypass the proxy?
rows.answer: The decision is made by should_bypass_proxies(url, no_proxy) in src/requests/utils.py:810-870. It first parses the URL and returns True immediately if the URL has no hostname (e.g. file:// URLs). If a no_proxy value is provided (or read from the NO_PROXY/no_proxy environment variable, preferring lowercase), it splits it on commas and checks the hostname: for IPv4 addresses it matches either a CIDR network via address_in_network or an exact plain-IP match; for other hosts it compares the hostname (and hostname:port when a port is present) against each entry, both as an exact match and as a suffix match after prepending a dot (so '.example.com' matches 'sub.example.com'). If no no_proxy match is found, it falls back to the platform proxy_bypass(hostname) (on Windows this checks the registry ProxyOverride via proxy_bypass_registry, src/requests/utils.py:96-146), returning True if that reports a bypass. Otherwise it returns False. This function is used by get_environ_proxies (src/requests/utils.py:873-908), which returns an empty dict when bypassing, and by resolve_proxies (src/requests/utils.py:911-962), which only applies environment proxies when trust_env is set and should_bypass_proxies is False.

arguments.query: bypass proxy URL no_proxy should bypass

rows.question: Where are proxy settings read from environment variables?
rows.answer: Proxy settings are read from environment variables in get_environ_proxies, which calls getproxies() (src/requests/utils.py:873-908). This is used by Session.merge_environment_settings to set the environment's proxies when trust_env is true (src/requests/sessions.py:831-886), and by resolve_proxies to merge environment proxies into the request's proxy mapping (src/requests/utils.py:911-962). The underlying getproxies and getproxies_environment functions are imported from urllib.request in src/requests/compat.py:83-115.

rows.question: How are query parameters URL-encoded into the request URL?
rows.answer: Query parameters are URL-encoded by PreparedRequest.prepare_url, which calls _encode_params on the params (src/requests/models.py:544-563). _encode_params converts the data into a list of (key, value) byte pairs via to_key_val_list, encoding each key and value as UTF-8, then returns urlencode(result, doseq=True) (src/requests/models.py:108-180). The resulting encoded string is appended to the existing query with an '&' separator if a query already exists, otherwise it becomes the query, and the full URL is rebuilt with urlunparse and passed through requote_uri (src/requests/models.py:544-563).

arguments.query: URL encode query parameters request URL

rows.question: How are multipart file uploads encoded?
rows.answer: Multipart file uploads are encoded by RequestEncodingMixin._encode_files, which builds the body for a multipart/form-data request: it converts data and files into key/value lists, wraps each file in a RequestField (with filename, optional content type and custom headers), calls make_multipart on each field, and finally calls encode_multipart_formdata to produce the body bytes and the multipart/form-data content type (src/requests/models.py:182-251). This is invoked from PreparedRequest.prepare_body when files are provided, and the resulting content type is set on the request headers if not already present (src/requests/models.py:603-652).

rows.question: How is the Content-Length of a request body computed?
rows.answer: The Content-Length is computed by PreparedRequest.prepare_content_length, which calls super_len(body) and, if a length is returned, sets the Content-Length header to that value; if the body is None and the method is not GET or HEAD, it sets Content-Length to 0 (src/requests/models.py:654-697). super_len determines the length by first encoding a str to utf-8 (for urllib3 2.x+), then using len(o) if the object has __len__, else o.len if it has a len attribute, else os.fstat(fileno).st_size if it has fileno, with a warning if the file is not opened in binary mode (src/requests/utils.py:160-199). For streamed/iterable bodies, prepare_body computes length via super_len and either sets Content-Length or falls back to Transfer-Encoding: chunked (src/requests/models.py:603-652).

rows.question: How are cookies from a response stored in the cookie jar?
rows.answer: Cookies from a response are stored in the cookie jar by extract_cookies_to_jar, which wraps the response's original HTTPMessage headers in a MockResponse and the PreparedRequest in a MockRequest, then calls jar.extract_cookies(res, req) so http.cookiejar parses and stores the Set-Cookie headers (src/requests/cookies.py:114-161).

arguments.query: store cookies from response in cookie jar

rows.question: How are session-level settings merged with per-request settings?
rows.answer: Session-level and per-request settings are merged by the merge_setting function, which prefers the explicit per-request value: if the session setting is None it returns the request setting, if the request setting is None it returns the session setting, and if both are mappings it builds a new dict from the session setting then updates it with the request setting, finally dropping any keys whose value is None (src/requests/sessions.py:76-124). This is applied in Session.prepare_request, which calls merge_setting for headers (using CaseInsensitiveDict), params, and auth, and merge_hooks for hooks, while cookies are merged separately via merge_cookies (src/requests/sessions.py:505-555). For proxies, stream, verify, and cert, Session.merge_environment_settings first gathers environment values when trust_env is set, then merges each with the corresponding session attribute using merge_setting (src/requests/sessions.py:831-886).

arguments.query: session-level settings merged with per-request settings

rows.question: How does a session pick which transport adapter handles a URL?
rows.answer: A session picks the transport adapter by iterating over its mounted adapters and returning the first one whose prefix matches the start of the URL, comparing case-insensitively; if none match it raises InvalidSchema (src/requests/sessions.py:831-886). Adapters are registered via mount, which stores the adapter under its prefix and reorders the adapters dict so longer prefixes come first, ensuring the most specific prefix wins (src/requests/sessions.py:888-905).

rows.question: Where are default headers such as User-Agent set?
rows.answer: Default headers such as User-Agent are set by the default_headers() function in src/requests/utils.py:911-962, which returns a CaseInsensitiveDict containing User-Agent (from default_user_agent()), Accept-Encoding, Accept, and Connection. These are assigned to a Session's headers in Session.__init__ at src/requests/sessions.py:442-488 via self.headers = default_headers().

rows.question: How are HTTP header names handled case-insensitively?
rows.answer: HTTP header names are handled case-insensitively by the CaseInsensitiveDict class, which stores each header using its lowercased name as the lookup key while keeping the original cased key alongside the value (src/requests/structures.py:20-74). Setting an item uses self._store[key.lower()] = (key, value), and getting an item uses self._store[key.lower()][1], so queries and contains tests are case insensitive while iteration and keys() preserve the case of the last key set (src/requests/structures.py:20-74). Equality comparison is also case-insensitive by comparing lower_items() of both mappings (src/requests/structures.py:76-93). PreparedRequest.prepare_headers creates self.headers as a CaseInsensitiveDict and stores each header name converted via to_native_string (src/requests/models.py:565-574).

rows.question: How are event hooks such as the response hook dispatched?
rows.answer: Event hooks are dispatched by the dispatch_hook function, which takes a hook key (e.g. "response"), the hooks dictionary, and the hook data (the Response), then looks up the list of hooks for that key; if a single callable is given it is wrapped in a list, and each hook is called in order with the current data plus any extra kwargs, with the returned value replacing the data when it is not None (src/requests/hooks.py:31-48). Hooks are registered on a request via RequestHooksMixin.register_hook, which appends a callable or extends with an iterable of callables for a given event, raising ValueError for unsupported events (src/requests/models.py:254-281). The actual dispatch of the response hook happens in Session.send after the adapter returns the response, where it calls dispatch_hook("response", hooks, r, **kwargs) using the request's hooks (src/requests/sessions.py:752-799).

rows.question: Where is the Link header parsed into a dictionary?
rows.answer: The Link header is parsed into a dictionary by the `links` property on `Response`, which calls `parse_header_links` and builds a dict keyed by `rel` or `url` (src/requests/models.py:1091-1142). The underlying parsing into per-link dicts happens in `parse_header_links` (src/requests/utils.py:965-1005).

rows.question: How does raising for HTTP error status codes build its error message?
rows.answer: Response.raise_for_status builds the message by first normalizing self.reason: if it is bytes it tries to decode as utf-8 and falls back to iso-8859-1 on UnicodeDecodeError, otherwise it uses the reason as-is (src/requests/models.py:1144-1184). It then sets http_error_msg to an f-string of the form "{status_code} Client Error: {reason} for url: {url}" when 400 <= status_code < 500, or "{status_code} Server Error: {reason} for url: {url}" when 500 <= status_code < 600 (src/requests/models.py:1144-1184). If the message is non-empty it raises HTTPError with that message and the response attached (src/requests/models.py:1144-1184).

arguments.query: raise HTTP error status code error message

rows.question: How are connect and read timeouts passed down to urllib3?
rows.answer: In HTTPAdapter.send, the timeout argument is normalized into a urllib3 Timeout object (imported as TimeoutSauce from urllib3.util): if it is a tuple, the two values are unpacked as connect and read and passed to TimeoutSauce(connect=connect, read=read); if it is already a TimeoutSauce it is used as-is; otherwise a single value is used for both connect and read (src/requests/adapters.py:681-693). The resulting resolved_timeout is then passed to conn.urlopen as timeout=resolved_timeout (src/requests/adapters.py:695-748).

rows.question: Where are credentials loaded from the user's netrc file?
rows.answer: Credentials are loaded from the user's netrc file by get_netrc_auth, which checks the NETRC environment variable first and otherwise looks for ~/.netrc or ~/.netrc (NETRC_FILES) in the user's home directory (src/requests/utils.py:231-287). The file location is defined by NETRC_FILES = (".netrc", "_netrc") (src/requests/utils.py:74-74).

rows.question: What does `prepare_url` do with internationalized (IDNA) host names?
rows.answer: prepare_url IDNA-encodes the host when it contains non-ASCII characters: it checks unicode_is_ascii(host), and if false it calls self._get_idna_encoded_host(host), which uses idna.encode(host, uts46=True).decode("utf-8") and raises UnicodeError (surfaced as InvalidURL "URL has an invalid label.") on idna.IDNAError; for ASCII hosts it only rejects labels starting with "*" or "." (src/requests/models.py:483-542, src/requests/models.py:424-481).

rows.question: What does `requote_uri` do?
rows.answer: requote_uri re-quotes a URI by passing it through an unquote/quote cycle so it is fully and consistently quoted: it first unquotes only unreserved characters via unquote_unreserved and then quotes only illegal characters, keeping reserved, unreserved and '%' characters safe (src/requests/utils.py:704-723). If the URI cannot be unquoted (InvalidURL), it quotes the original URI directly, ensuring any unquoted '%' characters are properly escaped (src/requests/utils.py:716-723). It is used to normalize URLs, e.g. in PreparedRequest.prepare_url (src/requests/models.py:544-563) and when resolving redirects (src/requests/sessions.py:237-280).

rows.question: How does `rewind_body` work?
rows.answer: rewind_body moves a file-like request body's pointer back to its recorded starting position so it can be read again on redirect (src/requests/utils.py:1098-1155). It gets the body's seek method via getattr(prepared_request.body, "seek", None); if that exists and prepared_request._body_position is an integer, it calls body_seek(prepared_request._body_position), raising UnrewindableBodyError if an OSError occurs; otherwise it raises UnrewindableBodyError because the body cannot be rewound (src/requests/utils.py:1098-1155). The _body_position value is recorded in prepare_body by calling body.tell() before reading, or set to object() if tell() fails (src/requests/models.py:603-652). It is called from resolve_redirects when the request is rewindable, i.e. _body_position is not None and the headers contain Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding (src/requests/sessions.py:237-280, src/requests/sessions.py:282-307).

rows.question: What does `get_connection_with_tls_context` do?
rows.answer: get_connection_with_tls_context returns a urllib3 HTTPConnectionPool for a given PreparedRequest and TLS settings; it is intended only for use when subclassing HTTPAdapter, not for direct user code (src/requests/adapters.py:455-510). It asserts the request is prepared, selects a proxy via select_proxy, builds host and pool-key attributes through build_connection_pool_key_attributes (raising InvalidURL on ValueError), and then obtains the connection either from a proxy manager (validating the proxy URL and raising InvalidProxyURL if the host is missing) or from the default poolmanager, returning the resulting connection (src/requests/adapters.py:455-510).

rows.question: Explain `CaseInsensitiveDict.lower_items`.
rows.answer: CaseInsensitiveDict.lower_items returns a generator of (lowercased_key, value) tuples, like items() but with all keys lowercased (src/requests/structures.py:76-78). It iterates over self._store.items(), where each entry is a (lowerkey, (original_key, value)) pair, and yields (lowerkey, value) (src/requests/structures.py:76-78). It is used by __eq__ to compare two mappings case-insensitively by building dicts from lower_items of both sides (src/requests/structures.py:76-93).

rows.question: My Authorization header disappears after the server redirects me. Why?
rows.answer: requests deliberately strips the Authorization header on redirects to avoid leaking credentials. When a redirect happens, rebuild_auth checks whether the header should be removed via should_strip_auth and, if so, deletes it from the prepared request (src/requests/sessions.py:309-332). should_strip_auth returns True whenever the hostname changes, and also when the port or scheme changes on the same host, except for the special case of an http (port 80) to https (port 443) redirect on the same host, which is kept for backwards compatibility (src/requests/sessions.py:154-184). So if your redirect goes to a different host, or changes scheme/port (other than the http->https same-host case), the Authorization header is removed.

rows.question: response.text shows garbled characters for a page that has no charset in its headers
rows.answer: When the response has no charset in its headers, Response.text falls back to auto-detection: if self.encoding is None it uses self.apparent_encoding (guessed via charset_normalizer or chardet), and if that is also unavailable it decodes with utf-8 using errors='replace', which can produce garbled characters (src/requests/models.py:1034-1089). The encoding is taken from the content-type header via get_encoding_from_headers, which returns None when there is no charset parameter (src/requests/utils.py:569-630). To fix it, set r.encoding to the correct value before accessing r.text (src/requests/models.py:1034-1089).

rows.question: Uploading a file object that was partially read sends the wrong Content-Length
rows.answer: This is handled by super_len, which computes the length as the total file size minus the current position so a partially read file-like object reports only the remaining bytes. It records the current position via tell(), seeks to the end to get the total length, then seeks back to the original position, and finally returns max(0, total_length - current_position) (src/requests/utils.py:160-228). That value is used to set the Content-Length header in prepare_body (src/requests/models.py:603-652) and prepare_content_length (src/requests/models.py:654-697).

arguments.query: partially read file object wrong Content-Length upload
super_len partially read file content length

rows.question: I get a TooManyRedirects exception. Where is it raised?
rows.answer: TooManyRedirects is raised in SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects when the number of redirects reaches self.max_redirects (src/requests/sessions.py:186-235). The exception class itself is defined in src/requests/exceptions.py:102-162.

rows.question: Requests ignores my NO_PROXY environment variable
rows.answer: Requests does honor NO_PROXY, but only when the session trusts the environment (trust_env=True, the default). The check is done in should_bypass_proxies, which reads the no_proxy environment variable (lowercase preferred over uppercase) and returns True if the URL's hostname matches an entry in the comma-separated no_proxy list (exact host, host:port, or a suffix match), or if the platform's proxy_bypass reports a bypass (src/requests/utils.py:810-870). get_environ_proxies returns an empty dict when should_bypass_proxies is true, so no proxy is applied (src/requests/utils.py:873-882). resolve_proxies only consults environment proxies when trust_env is true and the URL is not bypassed (src/requests/utils.py:911-937). If you set trust_env=False, or pass an explicit proxies dict that overrides the scheme, the NO_PROXY environment variable will not be consulted, which is the usual reason it appears to be ignored (src/requests/utils.py:911-937).

rows.question: A header value containing a newline raises InvalidHeader
How does closing a session release its transport adapters?
rows.answer: Session.close() iterates over the values of self.adapters and calls close() on each one, which disposes of the adapter's internal state (src/requests/sessions.py:883-886). For the default HTTPAdapter, close() clears the pool manager and any active proxy managers, closing pooled connections (src/requests/adapters.py:556-563). The base BaseAdapter.close() is a no-op stub that subclasses override (src/requests/adapters.py:152-155).

rows.question: How are outgoing request headers validated and stored case-insensitively?
rows.answer: Outgoing request headers are validated and stored case-insensitively in PreparedRequest.prepare_headers, which creates a CaseInsensitiveDict, iterates over the provided header items, calls check_header_validity on each (name, value) pair, and stores the value under to_native_string(name) (src/requests/models.py:565-574). The case-insensitive storage is provided by CaseInsensitiveDict, which remembers the case of the last key set but performs lookups and contains tests case-insensitively (src/requests/structures.py:20-74). The actual per-part validation is done by _validate_header_part, which selects a regex validator for the name or value based on whether the part is str or bytes, raises InvalidHeader for non-str/bytes input, and raises InvalidHeader if the part fails the validator due to invalid leading whitespace, reserved characters, or return characters (src/requests/utils.py:1098-1155).

rows.question: How does closing a response release its underlying connection?
rows.answer: Response.close() releases the connection by first closing the underlying raw stream if the content has not been consumed, then calling the raw object's release_conn method to return the connection to the pool (src/requests/models.py:1144-1184).

rows.question: How is a dictionary converted to a cookie jar while respecting overwrite?
rows.answer: cookiejar_from_dict builds a RequestsCookieJar (or uses the provided jar), collects the names of cookies already in the jar, then for each key in the dictionary it calls set_cookie with create_cookie only when overwrite is True or the name is not already present in the jar (src/requests/cookies.py:579-601).

arguments.query: dictionary converted to cookie jar overwrite

rows.question: Which Python versions does requests officially support?
rows.answer: Requests officially supports Python 3.10+ (README.md:30-38).

rows.question: How do I install requests?
rows.answer: Run `python -m pip install requests` in your terminal (docs/user/install.rst:10-15). Alternatively, clone the source from GitHub and install it with `python -m pip install .` (docs/user/install.rst:17-36).

rows.question: What are the runtime dependencies of requests?
rows.answer: The runtime dependencies of requests are charset_normalizer>=2,<4, idna>=2.5,<4, urllib3>=1.26,<3, and certifi>=2023.5.7 (pyproject.toml:1-24).

rows.question: How do I run the test suite?
rows.answer: Run the test suite with `make test`, which executes `python -m pytest tests` (Makefile:1-27). For CI-style runs with a JUnit report, use `make ci`, which runs `python -m pytest tests --junitxml=report.xml` (Makefile:1-27). You can also run coverage with `make coverage` (Makefile:1-27).

rows.question: How do I set a timeout on a request?
rows.answer: Pass the timeout parameter to the request call. A single value applies to both the connect and read timeouts, e.g. requests.get('https://github.com', timeout=5) (docs/user/advanced.rst:1086-1117). To set them separately, pass a tuple (connect, read), e.g. requests.get('https://github.com', timeout=(3.05, 27)) (docs/user/advanced.rst:1086-1117). You can also pass timeout=None to wait forever (docs/user/advanced.rst:1119-1137). The timeout is not a limit on the entire response download; an exception is raised if no bytes are received on the socket for timeout seconds (docs/user/quickstart.rst:529-549).

arguments.query: set a timeout on a request

rows.question: How do I use HTTP basic authentication?
rows.answer: To use HTTP Basic Auth, import HTTPBasicAuth and pass it as the auth argument: from requests.auth import HTTPBasicAuth; basic = HTTPBasicAuth('user', 'pass'); requests.get('https://httpbin.org/basic-auth/user/pass', auth=basic) (docs/user/authentication.rst:13-33). You can also use the shorthand tuple form, which is exactly the same: requests.get('https://httpbin.org/basic-auth/user/pass', auth=('user', 'pass')) (docs/user/authentication.rst:13-33). If no auth argument is given, Requests will try to read credentials for the hostname from the user's netrc file and send the request with HTTP Basic Auth (docs/user/authentication.rst:36-56).

rows.question: How do I configure proxies?
rows.answer: You can configure proxies in three ways. Per request, pass a proxies dict to any request method, e.g. requests.get('http://example.org', proxies={'http': 'http://10.10.1.10:3128', 'https': 'http://10.10.1.10:1080'}) (docs/user/advanced.rst:578-614). For a whole session, set session.proxies.update(proxies) on a requests.Session, though note these values may be overwritten by environmental proxies, so explicitly passing proxies per request is safer (docs/user/advanced.rst:578-614). Or use standard environment variables http_proxy, https_proxy, no_proxy, and all_proxy (uppercase variants also supported), e.g. export HTTP_PROXY="http://10.10.1.10:3128" (docs/user/advanced.rst:614-645). For HTTP Basic Auth use the http://user:password@host/ syntax in any entry (docs/user/advanced.rst:614-645). For a specific scheme and host, use the scheme://hostname form as the key, e.g. proxies = {'http://10.20.1.128': 'http://10.10.1.10:5323'} (docs/user/advanced.rst:647-691). For SOCKS proxies, install the extra with pip install 'requests[socks]' and use schemes like socks5:// or socks5h:// (the latter resolves DNS on the proxy server) (docs/user/advanced.rst:647-695).

rows.question: How do I verify SSL certificates or turn verification off?
rows.answer: Requests verifies SSL certificates for HTTPS requests by default, and throws an SSLError if it cannot verify the certificate (docs/user/advanced.rst:211-244). To verify against a specific CA, pass verify the path to a CA_BUNDLE file or a directory of trusted CA certificates, e.g. requests.get('https://github.com', verify='/path/to/certfile'), or set it persistently on a session with s.verify = '/path/to/certfile' (docs/user/advanced.rst:211-244). If verify points to a directory, it must have been processed with the c_rehash OpenSSL utility (docs/user/advanced.rst:211-244). You can also set the trusted CAs via the REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE environment variable, with CURL_CA_BUNDLE as a fallback (docs/user/advanced.rst:211-244). To turn verification off, set verify to False, e.g. requests.get('https://kennethreitz.org', verify=False); note this accepts any TLS certificate and ignores hostname mismatches and expired certificates, making the application vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks, so it is only recommended for local development or testing (docs/user/advanced.rst:243-252).

rows.question: What is a Session object and why would I use one?
rows.answer: A Session object is a Requests session that provides cookie persistence, connection-pooling, and configuration (src/requests/sessions.py:395-440). You would use one to keep cookies, headers, authentication, proxies, and other settings consistent across multiple requests, and it can be used as a context manager (src/requests/sessions.py:395-440).

rows.question: How do I contribute a change to requests?
rows.answer: To contribute a change to requests, first read the Contributor's Guide and the AI Policy before opening any issues or proposing pull requests (.github/CONTRIBUTING.md:1-8). The Contributor's Guide lays out guidelines and advice for contributing, and is split into sections based on the type of contribution you're thinking of making (docs/dev/contributing.rst:1-23). Note that maintainers have the last word on whether a contribution is suitable, and contributions may be rejected if they do not suit the project's current goals (docs/dev/contributing.rst:49-59). You must also comply with the AI Policy: every contribution must be backed by a human who owns the copyright, no LLM bots in Co-authored-by, and no unsupervised agentic tools (.github/AI_POLICY.md:1-27).
